name: Orion

placement_rationale.text: 7 km marks Orion's forward ISR/strike orbit, not the airfield its 550 kg, runway-dependent airframe actually operates from — like Forpost-RU and its Ukrainian counterpart Bayraktar TB2 in this same catalog, a MALE-class platform this size is normally based well to the rear and reaches the front via its stated 250 km comms range. 7 km sits inside doctrine.md §2's drone-dense corridor (~30 km either side of the front), plausible for the persistent overwatch-plus-strike role this asset's own employment_notes compare directly to TB2's. (Nudged 7→7.4 km from this category's shared round-number value so it doesn't literally coincide with side_b-uav-forpost-ru on the map's distance axis — a small, deterministic spread within the same band, not a new plausibility claim beyond what's already argued above.)

sources.label: The National Interest — Is the Orion UAV Russia's answer to Ukraine's Turkish drones?

characteristics: Strength: Class-leading endurance and altitude among Russian UAVs in this catalog, comparable in role to Western MALE drones like Bayraktar TB2
Limitation: High unit cost relative to the mass-produced smaller UAV types, making it a higher-value target if lost
Estimated quantity available: Small fleet; exact total not disclosed
employment_notes: Represents Russia's attempt to field a MALE-class strategic/operational reconnaissance-strike drone comparable to Bayraktar TB2, at a much higher unit cost than its small tactical drone fleet
contrast_vs_traditional: Orion fills the medium-altitude, long-endurance strike-reconnaissance role TB2 fills on the other side of the line — both platforms chasing the same traditional-airpower job of persistent overwatch plus precision strike without a pilot at risk, and both constrained by the same doctrine.md finding that whoever controls the lower sky over a sector, not either platform's specifications, decides how close it can safely operate.
